textTitles: The Tool Library at Blackford Yard
How a town keeps its water clean

paragraphs.text: Mobile library — timetable and rules. The van visits fourteen villages on a three-week cycle, and the stops for each week are printed on the card in the van and on the council page. Each stop lasts between thirty and fifty minutes; the van waits for the full time even when nobody is there, so a reader who arrives late in the slot is not left behind. Bad weather cancels a whole day rather than a stop, and a cancelled day is added to the end of the cycle.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The van carries about two thousand books, which are changed between cycles, and anything not on board can be requested and will arrive at your stop on the next visit. Borrowing limits are the same as at the branch libraries: twelve items, three weeks, two renewals. Audio books and large print are carried in quantity, because the readers who use this service are older on average than those who use a branch.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The van has a step and a handrail, and a ramp is carried for anybody who cannot manage the step; ask the driver, who will put it out. Readers who cannot leave the house at all may join the home delivery service instead, which brings a selection chosen from a short form about what you like and is run by volunteers. Fines are not charged on this service at all, and books returned damaged are replaced without argument unless the same reader does it repeatedly.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: B
texts.title: The Tool Library at Blackford Yard

paragraphs.text: The Tool Library at Blackford Yard. Members may borrow power tools, garden equipment and hand tools for up to a week. Membership costs £20 a year, or £8 for people receiving benefits, and includes as many loans as you like; there is no charge per item. We are open Thursday and Friday from 2 pm to 7 pm and Saturday from 9 am to 2 pm, and everything must be returned during opening hours rather than left outside the door.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Some items need a short demonstration before a first loan: the tile cutter, the floor sander, the chainsaw and the pressure washer. The demonstration takes ten minutes and is given at the counter; it is recorded against your membership, so it is needed once and not every time. Anybody under eighteen may not borrow the items on that list even with an adult present, and nobody may borrow the chainsaw without showing a certificate.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Tools are checked on return, and a tool that is blunt or has a worn part is repaired by us rather than charged to the borrower; a tool that has been used on the wrong material, which is usually obvious, is charged at the cost of the part. Consumables are not included: buy your own blades, discs and sandpaper, or purchase them at the counter at cost. If you need a tool longer than a week, ask before the return date and it is usually possible, unless somebody has reserved it.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: First aid at work: who does what. Every shift has at least one qualified first-aider, whose name is on the board by the door and on the intranet page; on a shift of more than fifty people there are two. The qualification lasts three years and is renewed by the company in working time. A first-aider is not a nurse and is trained to keep somebody safe until help arrives, which is the whole of the role and is enough in most incidents.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: If somebody is injured, send for the first-aider before doing anything else, and do not move the person unless leaving them creates a greater danger. The first-aid room is by the stores; the kits on the wall are checked monthly and the date is on the seal, so a broken seal means the kit has been opened and must be reported rather than quietly closed. Nothing may be taken from a kit for use at home, which sounds obvious and is the commonest reason kits are found empty.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Every treatment, however small, is written in the accident book on the day, with the time, what happened and what was done. The entry is made by the first-aider and signed by the injured person if they are able; a person who declines to sign is recorded as having declined, and nothing further is required of them. These records are confidential and are kept for the period the law requires, which is longer than most people expect.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Some events are reported beyond the site. An injury that stops somebody working for more than a week, any broken bone other than in a finger or toe, and any incident that could have caused serious harm go to the safety authority through the manager on duty, and the deadline for that report is short. Ambulances are called by the first-aider or the manager, never by the injured person’s colleague acting alone, because a second call from a different number delays the response rather than speeding it up.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Shift swaps and holiday cover. A swap between two employees of the same grade is agreed between them and recorded in the rota system by the person giving up the shift, at least forty-eight hours before the earlier of the two shifts. Nobody needs a manager’s permission for such a swap, and nobody may swap into a shift that would take them over the weekly hours limit; the system refuses the entry rather than relying on anybody to notice.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Where a swap cannot be found, the shift is offered to the cover list, which is a group of employees who have asked to be told about extra work. Cover is paid at the ordinary rate plus a quarter, and the offer goes out by message to the whole list at once rather than being telephoned around in an order that nobody can check. The first person to accept takes the shift, and accepting is binding in the same way as any other rota entry.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Holiday is requested through the same system, and the rules are about coverage rather than about who asks first. Each team has a maximum number of people off at one time, published for every week of the year; requests inside that limit are approved automatically, and requests that would exceed it go to the team leader, who decides by the published order of priority: booked-and-paid travel first, school holidays for those with children next, then length of service.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Two protections apply. A shift swap or a cover shift does not affect holiday entitlement, which accrues on contracted hours, so nobody loses by helping. And an employee who covers three or more extra shifts in a month may ask for a day in lieu instead of the supplement, which is granted unless the day requested is one of the weeks already at its coverage limit. The purpose of both rules is that helping out should never make somebody worse off than not helping.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: E
texts.title: How a town keeps its water clean

paragraphs.text: Clean water arrives through a tap with so little ceremony that it is easy to forget it is a manufactured product. Between a river and a kitchen there are usually six or seven separate processes, each removing a different kind of problem, and the order in which they are applied matters as much as the processes themselves. The system that results is the single public health measure that has saved more lives than any other, and it is almost entirely invisible. A resident notices it exactly twice: when the bill arrives and when something goes wrong.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first step is to take the water from the right place at the right time. Intakes are sited upstream of towns and away from the outfalls of others, and a works will stop drawing water altogether after heavy rain, when a river carries a month of field run-off in a day. Reservoirs help here as storage rather than as treatment: water that has stood for weeks is already cleaner, because particles settle and sunlight kills some of what is living in it.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Removing what is suspended comes next and is mostly chemistry rather than filtering. A coagulant is added and stirred fast, then slowly, which makes the invisible particles clump into flocs heavy enough to sink; the water then passes through sand, which catches what is left. Getting the dose right is a daily judgement that depends on the temperature and on what the river is carrying, and a plant with an experienced operator uses less chemical than one without. The savings are small on any one day and are the difference between a well-run works and an expensive one over a year.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Disinfection is the step that made the difference historically. Chlorine added at the end of the process kills the organisms that cause the diseases that once emptied cities, and a small residual is deliberately left in the water so that it continues to protect it through the pipes. That residual is why tap water tastes of something; a country that removes it entirely, as several do, must keep the pipe network in a condition that most cannot afford. The taste, in other words, is the price of tolerating older pipes, which is a trade most countries have made deliberately.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The newest problems are not microbes. Nitrate from farming, metals from old plumbing, and a long list of compounds from medicines and industry pass through conventional treatment largely unchanged, and removing them requires membranes or activated carbon, both of which are expensive and energy-hungry. Most countries treat this as a matter of limits and monitoring rather than of removal, on the reasoning that it is cheaper to keep a substance out of the river than to take it out of the water.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The pipes are the weak point and the part nobody photographs. A treatment works is a building that can be inspected; a network is thousands of kilometres of buried pipe, much of it older than anybody working on it, leaking between a fifth and a third of what enters it in many cities. Leakage is not only lost water: a pipe that leaks out can also draw in when the pressure drops, which is the route by which contamination reaches a supply that was clean when it left the works.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What decides whether water is safe is therefore management rather than technology. The processes have been understood for a century and the equipment can be bought; what fails is monitoring that is not done, a maintenance budget that is deferred, an operator who was never trained, and a report that goes to nobody. Investigations of outbreaks in wealthy countries find this pattern rather than an unknown pathogen, and the same investigations recommend the same dull things each time. Nothing in the list is difficult; everything in it competes for money with something more visible.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: For places without a network at all, the useful technologies are smaller and the constraint is the same. Household filters, chlorine tablets and solar disinfection all work in trials and all depend on somebody using them correctly every day for years; the schemes that succeed are those with a local supply chain and a person whose job it is, and the schemes that fail are those that delivered equipment and left. That is the same finding as in the pipes, written at a different scale.
paragraphs.label: H
